book_title: Chapter 1: How Azad Engineering Was Built — Precision Forging, Qualification & Capex Cycles
question: How did a 1983 Hyderabad industrial entity transform after 2008 into a qualified Tier-1 supplier of rotating airfoils for global turbine and aerospace OEMs, and what capital cycles shaped its current balance sheet?

epigraph.quote: In mission-critical engineering, the barrier is rarely the machine tool you can buy with capital; it is the three-to-five years of metallurgical proof you must earn before an OEM lets your part spin inside a turbine.
epigraph.author: Institutional Underwriting Maxim

web_blocks.title: From 1983 Incorporation to Rakesh Chopdar's 2008 Pivot

web_blocks.html: Azad Engineering Limited was incorporated in 1983 [1][2]. Its modern industrial identity began in 2008. First-generation entrepreneur Rakesh Chopdar took the helm in Hyderabad and pivoted toward ultra-precision, life-critical rotating components [2]. At that time, most Indian precision shops chased low-complexity, high-volume automotive or general industrial job work. Switching costs were minimal, and domestic price competition capped margins. Chopdar spotted a structural gap in the global supply chain. Western and Japanese original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) in power generation, oil and gas, and aerospace faced aging machining capacity and rising labor costs. They also struggled with multi-year lead times for complex 3D airfoils and turbine blades [2][5].

Entering that supply chain required more than buying 5-axis CNC machines and bidding on tenders. Global turbine and aero-engine OEMs put prospective vendors through 3-to-5-year qualification cycles. These audits test metallurgical integrity, destructive and non-destructive testing (NDT), AS9100 quality systems, and NADCAP special-process accreditations [5]. Early units in IDA Jeedimetla (Hyderabad) served as Azad's proving ground. There, the team built its engineering bench and mastered exotic alloys like Inconel, Waspaloy, titanium, and specialized martensitic stainless steels [2][5]. Over the next fifteen years, Azad qualified more than 1,700 distinct part numbers. That intangible asset cannot be replicated quickly by a well-funded entrant [5].

Between 2010 and 2023, Azad climbed the qualification ladder across four global sectors. These are thermal/gas/nuclear energy turbines, oil and gas equipment, commercial/defense aerospace, and domestic defense propulsion [2][4][5]. Management avoided relying on a single anchor client. Instead, it built overlapping Long-Term Contract and Price Agreements (LTCPAs) with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI), GE Vernova (and legacy GE Steam Power), and Siemens Energy. The roster also includes Baker Hughes, Rolls-Royce, Honeywell, Eaton, and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) [4][10][11][12]. By FY21, consolidated revenue reached ₹123 Cr with a 23% operating profit margin (OPM) [1]. Qualified part families then shifted from first-article inspection into serial production. Revenue jumped to ₹194 Cr in FY22 (32% OPM) and ₹252 Cr in FY23 (29% OPM) [1].

That pre-IPO growth phase exposed the financing tension of precision aerospace and turbine manufacturing. Exotic superalloy bar stock and forgings must be procured months ahead of delivery. Global OEM receivables also carry long export credit terms. As a result, Azad's borrowings climbed from ₹88 Cr in Mar 2021 to ₹197 Cr in Mar 2022 and ₹301 Cr in Mar 2023 [1]. Interest expense surged from ₹5 Cr in FY21 to ₹52 Cr in FY23. That interest burden compressed FY23 net profit to ₹8 Cr despite ₹72 Cr in operating profit [1]. Early institutional backers—including Piramal Structured Credit Opportunities Fund and DMI Finance—funded this private phase. Pre-IPO angel investors such as Sachin Tendulkar (who invested roughly ₹5 Cr in early 2023), VVS Laxman, Saina Nehwal, and PV Sindhu also joined ahead of listing [9].

web_blocks.title: The Two Capital Raises: Dec 2023 IPO and Mar 2025 QIP

web_blocks.html: In December 2023, Azad Engineering completed a ₹740 Cr Initial Public Offering (IPO). It comprised a ₹240 Cr fresh issue and a ₹500 Cr Offer for Sale (OFS) by Piramal, DMI Finance, and promoter Rakesh Chopdar [9]. Of the fresh proceeds, ₹138.19 Cr went to debt repayment and ₹60.40 Cr went to capital expenditure. Another ₹24.17 Cr funded general corporate purposes [9]. Deleveraging was immediate. Total borrowings dropped from ₹301 Cr in Mar 2023 to ₹39 Cr in Mar 2024. Interest expense eased to ₹18 Cr by FY25. Consolidated revenue accelerated to ₹341 Cr in FY24 (+35% YoY) and ₹457 Cr in FY25 (+34% YoY) [1].

Soon after the IPO deleveraged the balance sheet, a wave of mega-contracts arrived. Cumulative multi-year OEM agreements topped ₹3,200 Cr, and the rolling order book reached ~₹6,500 Cr [3][10]. Fulfilling that backlog required a step-change in dedicated plant capacity. Between February 25 and March 3, 2025, Azad executed a ₹700 Cr Qualified Institutional Placement (QIP). It issued 5,468,750 shares at ₹1,280 per share [8]. The QIP allocated ₹525.00 Cr to capital expenditure, ₹156.21 Cr to general corporate purposes, and ₹18.79 Cr to issue expenses [8]. From Dec 2023 to Sep 2026, promoter shareholding stepped down from 65.90% to 55.84% via OFS and QIP dilution. Over the same span, FII ownership rose from 4.68% to 12.70%, and DII ownership grew from 5.71% to 10.40% [1].

web_blocks.takeaway: Azad's history is defined by two distinct engines: patient 3-to-5-year OEM qualification moats on the shop floor, and heavy equity/debt capital raises every 15–24 months to fund dedicated plant blocks ahead of commercial ramp-up.

web_blocks.title: The Tuniki Bollaram Expansion & Post-QIP Capex Cycle (FY25–H1 FY27)

web_blocks.html: Armed with QIP proceeds, Azad received a July 2025 credit rating upgrade from CARE Ratings to CARE A; Stable / CARE A2+ [5]. Management then built a Centre of Excellence at Tuniki Bollaram near Hyderabad [16]. Between March 2025 and September 2026, Azad commissioned six customer-dedicated lean manufacturing facilities spanning 44,800 square meters. These include a 7,200 sq. m. plant for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (Mar 2025) and a 7,600 sq. m. Steam Power plant for GE Vernova (Apr 2025). Azad also opened a 7,200 sq. m. plant for Siemens Energy (Sep 2025) and a 7,600 sq. m. plant for Baker Hughes (Apr 2026). Two more exclusive 7,600 sq. m. plants for GE Vernova opened on September 28, 2026 [16][17]. Fixed assets surged from ₹257 Cr in Mar 2024 to ₹779 Cr in Mar 2026 and ₹989 Cr by Sep 2026, with ₹212 Cr in CWIP [1]. Borrowings climbed back to ₹474 Cr in Mar 2026 and ₹578 Cr in Sep 2026. That sets up this dossier's central tension: strong revenue and EBITDA growth paired with heavy capital and working-capital absorption [1].

web_blocks.title: Key Cycle Insight: Qualification Lag vs. Capex Front-Loading
paragraphs: Unlike software or asset-light consumer businesses, precision turbine manufacturing requires Azad to build dedicated clean-room bays, install 5-axis CNC cells, and hold raw superalloy inventory months before OEM delta qualifications clear for full-rate serial billing. That structural lag explains why operating profit surged 8x between FY21 (₹28 Cr) and FY26 (₹225 Cr) even as free cash flow remained deeply negative throughout the buildout.

web_blocks.title: Governance, Institutional Ownership & Capital Allocation Track Record

web_blocks.html: Shareholding since listing reflects Azad's shift from a private credit-backed shop into an institutional industrial platform [1][9]. Promoter Rakesh Chopdar's stake moved from 65.90% at the December 2023 IPO to 60.32% in March 2025. By September 2026, it stood at 55.84% following QIP dilution [1]. Over that window, Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) raised their stake from 4.68% to 12.70%, peaking at 16.16% in June 2025. Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs) increased their holding from 5.71% to 10.40%. The shareholder base broadened from 1,35,090 to 1,49,134 [1]. Crucially, Azad paid zero dividends across FY21–FY26 [1]. Management retained 100% of earnings plus ₹940 Cr of gross IPO/QIP fresh equity [8][9] to fund the Tuniki Bollaram Centre of Excellence. That zero-dividend policy reflects a capital-intensive buildout phase. Investors in Azad are backing long-term plant scale rather than near-term cash payouts.

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Azad Engineering without getting swept up in headline narratives about aerospace and clean energy, you and I have to start in 2008, not 2023. Although the corporate shell dates back to 1983, the business we are analyzing today was forged when Rakesh Chopdar took over a modest Hyderabad industrial outfit in 2008 and made a contrarian bet. At a time when most Indian machine shops were chasing high-volume automotive brackets and tractor parts—businesses where a competitor across the street can undercut your quote by three percent next quarter—Chopdar decided to chase the hardest, slowest, most unforgiving corner of global manufacturing: rotating airfoils and mission-critical turbine components.

Why is that corner so unforgiving? Picture a heavy-duty gas turbine generating electricity or a commercial jet engine cruising at thirty-five thousand feet. Inside that hot section, blades and vanes made from nickel-based superalloys and titanium spin thousands of times a minute under extreme thermal stress. If a single blade fractures because of a microscopic metallurgical flaw or a machining tolerance that drifted by a few microns, the entire turbine destroys itself. Because the cost of failure is catastrophic, global original equipment manufacturers—names like Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Rolls-Royce, and Baker Hughes—do not hand out purchase orders to the lowest bidder. Instead, they put a prospective supplier through a three-to-five-year qualification gauntlet.

For more than a decade at its legacy Jeedimetla facilities in Hyderabad, Azad endured that gauntlet. Every part number required first-article prototyping, destructive metallurgical testing, non-destructive ultrasonic and fluorescent penetrant inspection, and process-level audits under AS9100 and NADCAP standards. By the time Azad came to the public markets, it had qualified more than 1,700 distinct part numbers across energy, oil and gas, and aerospace. That qualification library is the bedrock of the company's moat. You can buy a five-axis CNC machine with a bank loan tomorrow; you cannot buy five years of signed-off OEM engineering trust.

As those qualified parts moved from trial batches into multi-year serial production, Azad's top line began compounding rapidly. Consolidated sales rose from ₹123 crore in FY21 to ₹194 crore in FY22 and ₹252 crore in FY23, while operating margins expanded from 23 percent to the high-twenties and thirties. Yet if you look closely at the pre-IPO balance sheet, you see the recurring shadow that follows this business model everywhere. Exotic superalloy bars and forgings have long import lead times, and global OEMs take months to inspect and settle export invoices. By March 2023, borrowings had swelled to ₹301 crore, interest costs ate ₹52 crore out of ₹72 crore in operating profit, and net profit shrank to just ₹8 crore. Private credit funds like Piramal and DMI Finance—alongside pre-IPO angel backers including Sachin Tendulkar—kept the growth engine funded until the December 2023 IPO.

The ₹740 crore IPO in December 2023—₹240 crore in fresh equity and ₹500 crore in secondary sales—gave Azad a clean reset. Using ₹138.19 crore of fresh proceeds to pay down debt, management cut borrowings from ₹301 crore down to ₹39 crore by March 2024. Revenue jumped to ₹341 crore in FY24 and ₹457 crore in FY25, with operating margins reaching 35 percent. For a brief moment, it looked like the balance sheet had turned asset-light.

Then came the next wave of global demand. Cumulative long-term contracts with MHI, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Baker Hughes, and Rolls-Royce pushed Azad's rolling order book toward ₹6,500 crore. To fulfill that backlog, existing Jeedimetla bays operating near 90 percent utilization were nowhere near enough. So in March 2025, Azad returned to institutional investors for a ₹700 crore Qualified Institutional Placement at ₹1,280 per share, earmarking ₹525 crore directly for capital expenditure. Promoter ownership stepped down from 65.90 percent at IPO to 55.84 percent by September 2026 as institutional FII and DII investors stepped in to fund the buildout.

Over the eighteen months from March 2025 through September 2026, Azad executed an extraordinary physical expansion at Tuniki Bollaram outside Hyderabad: six customer-dedicated lean manufacturing plants covering 44,800 square meters—one for MHI, three for GE Vernova, one for Siemens Energy, and one for Baker Hughes. Fixed assets nearly quadrupled from ₹257 crore in March 2024 to ₹989 crore by September 2026, and borrowings climbed right back up to ₹578 crore. That is the core rhythm of Azad Engineering's history: a world-class engineering moat that wins multi-billion-rupee OEM commitments, paired with relentless capital intensity that repeatedly tests the balance sheet before the cash flows arrive.

Notice also what happened to the cap table during this transformation. In December 2023, promoters held 65.90 percent of the company, while foreign and domestic institutions together held just over 10 percent. By September 2026, after the March 2025 QIP and institutional accumulation, promoter ownership settled at 55.84 percent, while FIIs held 12.70 percent and DIIs held 10.40 percent. Every rupee of retained profit—zero dividends were paid from FY21 through FY26—and nearly ₹940 crore of gross fresh equity from the IPO and QIP went straight into CNC cells, clean-room bays, and superalloy working capital.

This history leaves you with a clear framing for the rest of our audit. Azad is not a turnaround story or a newly minted startup; it is an eighteen-year precision engineering franchise that spent its first fifteen years earning OEM trust and its last three years building the physical capacity to monetize a ₹6,500 crore order book. Whether that physical capacity converts into high-return cash flow is the central question we will test chapter by chapter.

Pause for a moment to appreciate how unusual that 2008-to-2026 arc really is inside Indian manufacturing. Most domestic machine shops never escape low-margin job-work for local automotive or general engineering clients because they lack the metallurgical discipline and balance-sheet patience to endure three-to-five-year OEM qualification cycles without immediate revenue. Rakesh Chopdar made the opposite bet: he absorbed years of pre-revenue audit scrutiny from General Electric, Siemens, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and Rolls-Royce, knowing that once a part number is frozen into a turbine or aero-engine bill of materials, switching suppliers is prohibitively risky for the OEM. That patient foundation explains why revenue compounded at 37% annually after FY21—and also why capital intensity has remained permanently high as each new OEM win demanded a dedicated, ring-fenced facility at Tuniki Bollaram.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Qualification Moat vs. The Capital Treadmill
book_callouts.text: When you study precision manufacturers like Azad, it is easy to fall in love with the 1,700 qualified parts and the marquee OEM logos. Those assets are real. But notice the pattern across 2021–2026: every time Azad wins a bigger seat at the global table, it must first spend hundreds of crores on dedicated plants, superalloy inventory, and working capital long before the customer's cash hits the bank. Keep that tension front and center as we examine the segments and cash flows.

book_callouts.title: MENTAL MODEL: Front-Loaded Capex with Delta-Qualification Lag
book_callouts.text: In dedicated OEM manufacturing, commissioning a new 7,600 sq. m. plant does not flip a revenue switch on Day 1. The customer must run 'delta qualifications' on the new machines and lines—verifying that parts cut in the new bay match the metallurgical and dimensional tolerances of the legacy bay. During that 6-to-12-month lag, depreciation, power, and skilled-engineer payroll hit the P&L immediately while revenue ramps slowly.

book_subsections.title: From Hyderabad Job-Shop to Global Tier-1: The Capital Cycle Lens
paragraphs: Every great industrial story moves through distinct capital cycles, and Azad Engineering is currently traversing its third major phase. In Phase 1 (2008–2020), the company funded early OEM qualifications and precision CNC machines through promoter capital, bank debt, and private-equity backing from Piramal Structured Credit, accepting thin early returns while building a 1,400-plus part catalog. In Phase 2 (2021–2024), those qualifications unlocked explosive 37% revenue compounding and took the company public in December 2023, briefly slashing borrowings from ₹301 crore to ₹39 crore.

In Phase 3 (2024–2026), management pivoted back into aggressive physical expansion—raising ~₹700 crore via its March 2025 QIP and adding six dedicated Tuniki Bollaram plants to capture a ₹6,500 crore rolling order book. Historically, Phase 3 buildouts are the riskiest moment for public shareholders: the balance sheet swells before asset turns normalize, and only disciplined execution in Phase 4 determines whether that capex earns 20%+ ROCE or remains trapped in working capital.
